nameStory: Many-seeded Goosefoot gets its name from two distinctive features that early botanists noticed. The leaves are shaped somewhat like a goose's webbed foot, giving the whole goosefoot family its common name. The 'many-seeded' part refers to this plant's prolific seed production - it can produce thousands of tiny seeds from a single plant!
description: Many-seeded Goosefoot is a small, weedy annual plant that most people overlook as they walk by. It grows low to the ground, typically reaching only 6-18 inches tall, with a sprawling, branching habit that forms loose mats. The small, oval leaves are alternate and have a distinctive pale green color, while tiny greenish flowers cluster along the stems. This humble plant belongs to the same family as spinach and quinoa, though you'd never guess it from its modest appearance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small oval leaves that feel smooth and slightly waxy to the touch, with a distinctive pale green or blue-green color that stands out from other weedy plants

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, spreading plant that branches extensively near the base, forming loose mats rather than growing upright like many weeds

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, inconspicuous greenish flowers that lack petals and cluster in small groups along the stems - you'll need to look closely to even notice them

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Produces abundant tiny, dark seeds that feel like fine grit between your fingers and can cover the ground around mature plants

habitat: Many-seeded Goosefoot thrives in disturbed soils and waste places throughout New England, though it's quite rare here. Look for it in cultivated fields, garden edges, roadsides, and areas where the soil has been recently turned or compacted. It prefers rich, nitrogen-rich soils and full sun to partial shade.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring when soil warms up, producing small seedlings with the characteristic pale oval leaves.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow rapidly and produce their tiny greenish flowers throughout the summer months, often blooming continuously from July onward.
seasonality.fall: Seed production peaks in late summer and early fall, with plants turning yellowish as they mature and begin to die back.
seasonality.winter: Plants die completely with the first hard frost, leaving behind thousands of seeds that will germinate the following spring.

funFact: Despite being called Many-seeded Goosefoot, this plant is actually the sole member of its own genus - it's so unique that botanists moved it out of the large Chenopodium genus and gave it its very own scientific name, Lipandra, making it a botanical 'only child'!
confusionNotes: Many-seeded Goosefoot can be confused with other goosefoot species (Chenopodium), but its low, mat-forming growth habit and distinctive pale blue-green leaf color help distinguish it. Remember: if it's sprawling flat rather than growing upright, and the leaves look almost powdery pale green, you've likely found Many-seeded Goosefoot.
contextualKnowledge: This plant was recently moved from the genus Chenopodium to its own genus Lipandra, so you might find it listed under either name in older field guides. The name change reflects new genetic research showing it's quite different from other goosefoot species, despite looking similar.
compareHints: Since Many-seeded Goosefoot is the only Lipandra species in our region, compare it with true goosefoot species (Chenopodium). Unlike its upright-growing Chenopodium cousins, Many-seeded Goosefoot sprawls along the ground in mats. It also has a more consistently pale, blue-green leaf color compared to the variable green shades of other goosefoot species.
